q-84054.name: Question 1
q-84054.problem: Consider a linear transformation $T:{R}^{6}\to {R}^{6}.$ If $\text{nullity}(T)=0$ then $\text{rank}(T)=$
q-84054.worked_solution:
According to the rank-nullity theorem, if $T:{R}^{n}\to {R}^{n},$ then

$$
\text{rank}(T)+\text{nullity}(T)=n.
$$

For the given transformation, we have $n=6.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{rank}(T)+\text{nullity}(T) & =n \\ \text{rank}(T)+0 & =6 \\ \text{rank}(T) & =6-0 \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

q-141434.name: Question 6
q-141434.worked_solution:
Solving $x-2y=0$ for $x,$ we get $x=2y.$ Solving $3u+v=0$ for $v,$ we get $v=-3u.$ Therefore, any vector from $\text{Im}(T)$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}2y \\ y \\ z \\ u \\ -3u\end{aligned}]=y{{[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{v}_{1}}+z{{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{v}_{2}}+u{{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 0 \\ 1 \\ -3\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{v}_{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

This means that $\text{Im}(T)=\text{Span}\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}\}.$ Therefore, $\text{rank}(T)=3.$ 

Finally, according the rank-nullity theorem, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{nullity}(T) & =5-\text{rank}(T) \\  & =5-3 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

a

Solving x−2y=0 for x, we get x=2y. Solving 3u+v=0 for v, we get v=−3u. Therefore, any vector from Im(T) can be written as [2yyzu−3u]=y[21000]⏟v1+z[00100]⏟v2+u[0001−3]⏟v3

q-141437.name: Question 7
q-141437.worked_solution:
Solving $x-2v=0$ for $x,$ we get $x=2v.$ Therefore, any vector from $\text{Ker}(T)$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}2v \\ y \\ z \\ 0 \\ v\end{aligned}]=y{{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{v}_{1}}+z{{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{v}_{2}}+v{{[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ 0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{v}_{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that $\text{Ker}(T)=\text{Span}\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}\}.$ Therefore, $\text{nullity}(T)=3.$ 

Finally, according the rank-nullity theorem, we obtain

$$

q-38146.name: Question 11
q-38146.problem:
Let $T:{R}^{3}\to {R}^{3}$ be a linear transformation with standard matrix $T$ whose columns are ${v}_{1},$
 ${v}_{2},$ and  ${v}_{3}.$

*If  $\text{dim}(\text{Span}\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}\})=1$, then $\text{__________}.$ *

Which of the following, if inserted into the blank space, would lead to a true statement?

I. $\text{nullity}(T)=2$

II. ${x}_{1}{v}_{1}+{x}_{2}{v}_{2}+{x}_{3}{v}_{3}=0$ has only the trivial solution

III. $\text{rank}(T)=2$
q-38146.worked_solution:
Since $T$ is a linear transformation from ${R}^{3}$ into ${R}^{3},$ the invertible matrix theorem states the following:

 $T$ is a bijection (an invertible transformation) $\,⟺\,\{\,\begin{aligned} & \text{Im}(T)={R}^{3} \\  & \text{rank}(T)=3 \\  & \text{Ker}(T)=\{0\} \\  & \text{nullity}(T)=0\end{aligned}$ 

Also, according to the rank-nullity theorem, 

$$
\text{rank}(T)+\text{nullity}(T)=3.
$$

With that in mind, let's examine each statement in turn.

- Statement I is true. Since $\text{dim}(\text{span}\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}\})=1$ this means that $\text{rank}(T)=1.$ According to the rank-nullity theorem, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{nullity}(T) & =3-\text{rank}(T) \\  & =3-1 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Also, according to the invertible matrix theorem the linear transformation $T$ cannot be a bijection.

- Statement II is false. Notice that ${x}_{1}{v}_{1}+{x}_{2}{v}_{2}+{x}_{3}{v}_{3}=0$ is equivalent to $Tx=0.$ Since $T$ is not invertible, the equation has non-trivial solutions.

- Statement III is false. From statement I, $\text{rank}(T)=1.$

Therefore, the correct option is "I only."

q-84063.name: Question 12
q-84063.problem:
Let $T:{R}^{3}\to {R}^{3}$ be a linear transformation whose standard matrix is $T.$ Which of the following statements are true?

I. If $\text{Im}(T)=\{[x,y,z]^{T}\,:\,x=0\}$ then $\text{nullity}(T)=1$

II. If $\text{Ker}(T)=\{[x,y,z]^{T}\,:\,y-2z=0,x+z=0\}$ then $\text{rank}(T)=2$

III. If ${v}_{1},$ ${v}_{2},$ and ${v}_{3}$ are the columns of $T$ and ${v}_{3}={v}_{1}-{v}_{2}$, then $\text{Ker}(T)\ne \{0\}$
q-84063.worked_solution:
Since $T$ is a linear transformation from ${R}^{3}$ into ${R}^{3},$ the invertible matrix theorem states the following:

 $T$ is a bijection (an invertible transformation) $\,⟺\,\{\,\begin{aligned} & \text{Im}(T)={R}^{3} \\  & \text{rank}(T)=3 \\  & \text{Ker}(T)=\{0\} \\  & \text{nullity}(T)=0\end{aligned}$ 

Also, according to the rank-nullity theorem, 

$$
\text{rank}(T)+\text{nullity}(T)=3.
$$

With that in mind, let's examine each statement in turn.

- Statement I is true. Any vector from $\text{Im}(T)$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]=y{{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{v}_{1}}+z{{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{v}_{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that $\text{Im}(T)=\text{Span}\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2}\}.$ Therefore, $\text{rank}(T)=2.$ Finally, according the rank-nullity theorem, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{nullity}(T) & =3-\text{rank}(T) \\  & =3-2 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is true. Solving $y-2z=0$ for $y,$ we get $y=2z.$ Solving $x+z=0$ for $x,$ we get $x=-z.$ Therefore, any vector from $\text{Im}(T)$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-z \\ 2z \\ z\end{aligned}]=z{{[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{v}_{1}}.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that $\text{Ker}(T)=\text{Span}\{{v}_{1}\}.$ Therefore, $\text{nullity}(T)=1.$ Finally, according the rank-nullity theorem, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{rank}(T) & =3-\text{nullity}(T) \\  & =3-1 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is true. If the columns of $T$ are such that ${v}_{3}={v}_{1}-{v}_{2},$ then the set of vectors $\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}\}$ is linearly dependent and therefore $\text{Im}(T)=\text{Col}(T)\ne {R}^{3}.$ Now, according to the matrix invertible theorem, we obtain that $\text{Ker}(T)\ne \{0\}.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III."

q-84061.name: Question 14
q-84061.problem:
Let $T:{R}^{3}\to {R}^{3}$ be a linear transformation whose standard matrix is $T.$ Which of the following statements are true?

I. $\text{rank}(T)=\text{nullity}(T)=3$

II. If $v=[1,0,0]^{T}$ is a solution of $T(x)=0$ then $T$ is invertible.

III. If there is not $u\in {R}^{3}$ such that $T(u)=[1,0,0]^{T},$ then $\text{rank}(T)=3.$
q-84061.worked_solution:
Since $T$ is a linear transformation from ${R}^{3}$ into ${R}^{3},$ the invertible matrix theorem states the following:

 $T$ is a bijection (an invertible transformation) $\,⟺\,\{\,\begin{aligned} & \text{Im}(T)={R}^{3} \\  & \text{rank}(T)=3 \\  & \text{Ker}(T)=\{0\} \\  & \text{nullity}(T)=0\end{aligned}$ 

Also, according to the rank-nullity theorem, 

$$
\text{rank}(T)+\text{nullity}(T)=3.
$$

With that in mind, let's examine each statement in turn.

- Statement I is false. According to the rank-nullity theorem, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{nullity}(T) & =3-\text{rank}(T) \\  & =3-3 \\  & =0 \\  & \ne 3.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. Since $v$ is a solution of $T(x)=0$, we have that $T(v)=0.$ Therefore $v\in \text{Ker}(T),$ thus according to the invertible matrix theorem $T$ is not invertible.

- Statement III is false. Since there is not $u\in {R}^{3}$ such that $T(u)=[1,0,0]^{T},$ we have that $T$ is not  a bijection (an invertible transformation). According to the invertible matrix theorem, $\text{rank}(T)\ne 3.$

Therefore, the correct option is "None of the statements are true."
